extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in media, social platforms, journalism, and online satire controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A news report describing a social-media platform's enforcement action against a satire/parody site for content Twitter considered hateful conduct, including the site's response and the article's editorial update. Useful for understanding how platforms treat satirical misgendering and account-lock procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter hateful conduct policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter determined the tweet promoting the Babylon Bee article “violates Twitter’s policy about violence against or harassment or threatening of other people on the basis of race, ethnicity, national origin, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, religious affiliation, age disability or serious disease.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protected characteristics include race, ethnicity, national origin, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, religious affiliation, age, disability, or serious disease. Content that is violent, harassing, or threatening toward people on these bases can violate policy and be subject to enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform enforcement mechanism for violative content
rubrics_metrics.description: When Twitter flags an account for hateful conduct, the account can be temporarily locked: the account owner is required to delete the violative Tweet before regaining access and cannot post new tweets while locked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement may be procedural (lock until deletion). The article illustrates this: the Bee's account was locked and the notification said the owner must delete the tweet to regain access. The platform may expect removal even from parody accounts; refusal to delete maintains the lock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire/parody does not automatically exempt content from harassment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Babylon Bee's story parodied a USA Today nomination but used language (e.g., calling Rachel Levine 'man of the year' and referring to Levine as 'he'/'his') that Twitter treated as hateful conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if content is labeled or presented as parody, platforms may still treat misgendering or targeting of a protected group/identity as harassment. Creators should be aware that satirical framing does not guarantee protection from moderation when content targets protected characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial update practice when identities are contested or sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Babylon Bee added an update to the article acknowledging that Levine identifies as a woman: “UPDATE: Since announcing this award, we’ve been told that Levine actually identifies as a woman.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may add updates to acknowledge a subject’s self-identification or correct factual points. In this case the site appended an update while also asserting the update did not change their satirical claim; such editorial choices can influence public perception but may not affect platform enforcement decisions.
